extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and patent attorneys handling infringement trials
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and practical guidance on what evidence is admissible and persuasive in patent infringement suits, and the kinds/strength of proof required to sustain or defeat the common statutory and equitable defenses. Focuses on expert testimony, proving prior art/novelty, utility, inventorship, reissues, abandonment, marking, and related defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of expert testimony in infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts may not testify directly on questions of law (e.g., whether there is infringement), but may testify on points of fact that control those legal questions, such as whether modes of operation of two machines are substantially the same or whether particular parts perform the same function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert can state factual comparisons (similarities/differences) or functional equivalence and the manner of performance; such factual testimony may be received to aid the court on issues of infringement even though the ultimate legal conclusion is for the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination limits for experts who discuss prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an expert in direct examination expounds the whole or part of the prior art, cross-examination may extend to the same sources; but where the expert confines testimony to similarities/differences between the plaintiff's patent and defendant's doings, he cannot be cross-examined on the prior art except by inquiring whether he considered it when forming his opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The limited inquiry (asking whether prior art was considered) is proper because it shows whether the expert treated the plaintiff's patent as primary or secondary; cross-examining experts on irrelevant characteristics merely to test knowledge or fairness is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/deposition limits under Equity Rule (SDNY)
rubrics_metrics.description: If expert testimony in patent causes is taken by affidavit, witnesses shall not give opinion as to the meaning of any patent claim or specification; testimony must be strictly confined to explanation of the operation of the relevant arts, processes, machines, manufactures or compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits or depositions containing matter forbidden by the rule or irrelevant/immaterial matter shall not be answered by the opposite party nor be the basis of cross-examination; the court may strike such matter at any stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's prima facie proof includes damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The last part of a plaintiff's prima facie evidence consists in proof of the amount of his damages, sometimes supplemented by evidence tending to show a greater amount should be entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed treatment of damages is large and covered in a separate chapter; note included here for symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for defence that patent claims unpatentable subject-matter (Defense 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence may be required to show that terms of art/science in the patent require the court to construe the patent as claiming a principle or other unpatentable subject rather than a patentable process, machine, manufacture, composition, or design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the patent plainly claims only a peculiar function of a described machine, this defense may be maintained without evidence outside the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for want of invention / state of the art (Defense 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence to show the state of the art is often required to demonstrate want of invention; courts will sometimes take judicial notice of general practices in an art, but where facts are not generally known expert evidence or proof of prior patents/printed publications is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When want of invention arises from complex combinations, proof should show prior existence of parts and that their union is an aggregation; where prior patents/publications are used to negative invention (not just novelty), expert testimony is generally necessary and may include experiments or other expert-acquired knowledge. Courts may resort to dictionaries and science books when evidence leaves meaning in doubt, consistent with judicial notice rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and proof of prior United States patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Duly certified copies of prior U.S. patents are admissible; printed copies from the Patent Office are commonly accepted in practice when no competency objection is raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certified bound volumes gratuitously distributed by the Commissioner are admissible; errors in a certified copy can be corrected by another carefully compared certified copy; letters patent must agree in name and date with pleadings when offered in proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and proof of prior foreign patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior foreign patents, when pleaded to negative novelty, may be proved prima facie by duly certified copies kept in the U.S. Patent Office; plenary proof requires certification by the corresponding foreign official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a certified copy is in error, it may be corrected by another certified copy from the same office; foreign patents are evidence of their own duration and absence of extension unless evidence shows otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of prior printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior printed publications must be proved by producing a specimen of the printed thing relied upon and by satisfactory evidence that it was published before the patent's date; parol testimony of the contents is generally inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A book or periodical that appears published on a specified date and that contains collateral evidence of genuineness, and is free from suspicion of alteration, may be received without direct testimony of publication date. Certificates by the Commissioner that a book was in the Patent Office library at a date are not evidence of that fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of prior knowledge or use (anticipation by prior use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge or use may be proved by testimony of persons who had such knowledge or who know of such prior use, covering existence, character, and date; testimony relying solely on memory is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desirable to produce the anticipating thing or a specimen and connect its history to indisputable events; where the article cannot be produced, reliance on multiple credible witnesses and simple, well-understood constructions strengthens the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of contradictory parol evidence and standard for want of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Parol evidence of an anticipating thing is likely to meet counter parol evidence; mere preponderance of evidence will not sustain a defense of want of novelty — that defense must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony that the witness purchased a license is generally little weight against a claim of prior use because purchase may reflect ignorance of legal defenses or preference to avoid litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's rebuttal when anticipating matter is proved
rubrics_metrics.description: When anticipating matter is undeniably proved, want of novelty is prima facie established; the plaintiff may rebut by proving he or his assignor made the invention at an earlier date, sometimes by certified copy of his original application but not by parol proof of filing time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the earlier fact is a tangible thing, production/ proof of loss/destruction and best obtainable evidence of its character are required; contemporaneous declarations of the patentee describing the invention before filing are competent (res gestae). Once plaintiff proves an earlier date, defendant cannot move the anticipating matter's date earlier than plaintiff's new date, but can attempt to disprove plaintiff's new date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of lack of utility / failure to perform claimed functions (Defense 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires evidence that the patented invention will not perform any function ascribed to it in the patent or that the function is not useful within the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may be testimony from someone skilled who in good faith attempted to make the thing work and failed, or theoretical demonstration of impossibility; the evidence must show total incapacity — imperfect operation or partial failure is insufficient. Practical/theoretical proof of lack of utility can be rebutted by testimony that the claimed result has been achieved. Evidence that the invention is morally dangerous or condemned by conventional ethics may show want of utility in the second sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of actual abandonment (Defense 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: May be supported by any competent evidence showing the inventor relinquished expectation of securing a patent and intended the invention to be free to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be direct or circumstantial, but must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt — a mere preponderance is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to apply within statutory period (Defense 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires proof that the inventor omitted to apply for a patent during the time allowed by statute for his particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact must be established beyond a reasonable doubt to succeed as a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to produce original application papers (Defense 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The seventh defense requires introduction of the original application papers or certified copies thereof and, except in very plain cases, expert testimony to explain outward embodiment of terms in the original patent and application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certified copies of original papers are central; experts often needed to interpret the original language and embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior conception and diligence (Defense 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for evidence that another conceived the invention prior to the patentee, used reasonable diligence to adapt and perfect it, and that the patentee obtained the patent surreptitiously or applied when the prior conceiver was not chargeable with laches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires proof of prior conception, diligence, and circumstances showing patentee's unjust acquisition of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of joint inventorship (Defense 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires proof that another was a joint inventor with the patentee of the claimed subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony must be strong to prevail because courts/juries tend to classify such evidence as mechanical assistance or suggested substitution of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of inequitable division of inventorship/interest (Defense 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: May be based on circumstances analogous to joint inventorship (e.g., sale of an undivided half interest then joint application) and other circumstances showing error or misjoinder of inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very clear and unequivocal evidence is necessary to support this defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct / intent to deceive Patent Office (Defense 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for proof that the patent contains less than whole truth or more than necessary with a fault arising from intention to deceive the public; intent is the gist of the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct positive evidence of intent is not required — circumstances sufficiently satisfying the jury that intent existed will suffice. A prima facie showing of intent may be rebutted by competent evidence, such as public disclosures by the inventor contemporaneous with issuance that would explain apparent omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of specification / enablement (Defense 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can be supported only by persons skilled in the art to which the invention pertains; a patent for a chemical composition/process cannot be overthrown by testimony of a mechanical expert, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A description that is sufficiently full, clear, concise, and exact to be effectually understood by any person skilled in that kind of machinery/subject is sufficient to meet this defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness / uncertainty in claim embodiment (Defense 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: May sometimes be sustained without evidence outside the letters patent, but prudence suggests fortifying the defense with expert testimony showing the outward embodiment of the claim is uncertain in character or extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony is advisable to show claim terms are uncertain; in some cases the patent alone may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known invalid claims and delay in disclaimer (Defense 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires proof that one or more claims are void for want of patentable subject-matter, invention, or novelty, and that the patentee long knew the facts making it invalid; absence of disclaimer is not always decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No disclaimer is necessary in absence of all three circumstances; delay to file disclaimer is unreasonable only if the fourth (presumably continued assertion despite known invalidity) exists. Proof of necessity for disclaimer and long-existing knowledge will not always sustain the defense when reasonable doubt exists whether the known facts made disclaimer necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue-based defenses where original patent showed deliberate omissions (Defense 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seldom supported by evidence that the original patent was inoperative or invalid due to defective or insufficient specification unless the error arose other than by inadvertence, accident, or mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defense requires evidence showing omissions were deliberate or careful, or omitted to secure the original patent; such evidence is often found in Patent Office correspondence and may be introduced as certified copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in applying for reissue (Defense 16)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can be supported by comparing the original patent with the reissue: if the reissue claims something the original did not and was applied for long after the original, this supports the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How long is ‘long’ depends on circumstances; different times have been held sufficient and are collated elsewhere; the burden is on the plaintiff to excuse delay beyond two years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial difference between reissue and original (Defense 17)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always requires the original patent and generally expert testimony showing that the outward embodiment of something claimed in the reissue is substantially different from anything described in the original and apparently intended to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge will not reject such expert testimony unless the case is so clear he would have decided it on demurrer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent by same inventor (Defense 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires introduction of the prior patent granted on the same inventor's application; usually does not require expert testimony unless phraseology renders understanding difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevail, the claim of the prior patent must be so clearly coextensive with the claim in suit that coextensiveness is apparent on the face of the documents; experts may be needed where claim language is obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of judicial repeal of a patent (Defense 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires introduction of an officially attested copy of the court record repealing the patent, or, if that record was destroyed, proof by a witness who examined and copied it when intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parol evidence is not admissible of a record of which only a part is lost; the existing part must be produced or proved by officially attested copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign patent to curtail U.S. patent term (Defense 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for a properly certified copy of the foreign patent relied upon; if parties offer no testimony, the court will determine identity of inventions by inspection of the two documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert evidence on identity will be received if offered; a foreign patent is evidence of its own duration and presumed not extended absent evidence to the contrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unmarked sales / notice and marking statute (Defense 21)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof that plaintiff made or sold specimens of the patented article without marking 'patented' together with the date of patent grants shifts the burden (if an accounting is prayed) to the plaintiff to show that before suit the defendant was duly notified of infringement and continued to infringe after such notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A voluntary statement by a third person that the defendant's doings infringe is not statutory notice, though it may be the beginning of suit. The marking defense does not apply to patents for processes because processes are used rather than made or sold.
